This paper examines a mass-supercritical focusing nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation defined in the exterior of a smooth, bounded obstacle with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. Building on previous work by the authors regarding positive ground states in the entire space, we demonstrate that the blow-up scenario adheres to a specific asymptotic profile as $|x| \to \infty$ and establish sufficient conditions prohibiting such blow-up behavior.

Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) facilitate the approximation of unknown physical phenomena governed by differential equations. Despite their potential, standard training strategies often yield poor solutions due to the non-convex nature of these problems, which leads to data undersampling in regions with significant solutions. To address this, we propose a new adaptive sampling technique for PINNs training, named RANG (Residual-based Adaptive Node Generation), which identifies critical areas within a physical domain that currently lack sufficient sample points. By continuously monitoring sub-region residuals and comparing them against threshold estimates, RANG triggers adaptive node generation in zones of high variation when necessary, without requiring a complete retraining process. This study validates the proposed method through three numerical examples involving heat conduction and two fluid dynamics scenarios, demonstrating its superior capability over conventional approaches in accelerating convergence rates and enhancing solution precision.

This research employs self-consistent coupling of the Wulfian total energy framework and the drift-diffusion system to investigate domain wall dynamics within ferroelectric FETs (FDFETs) and to examine how these dynamics influence electrostatics and device current. Our simulations reveal that in an n-channel FDFET, current flow originates from the negative intrinsic capacitance associated with the domain wall to confirm this finding, we establish a simplified equivalent circuit. Consequently, we integrate the negative capacitance mechanism into a comprehensive device simulator by incorporating the domain wall's profile, capacitance, and conductance, which clarifies the underlying physical mechanisms.

Software dependency management stands as a critical challenge within the contemporary software engineering landscape. In this study, we explore the propagation mechanisms of vulnerabilities through the entire cargo ecosystem. To facilitate this analysis, we built Dependency-Vulnerability Knowledge Graphs specific to each cargo, enabling direct visualization of dependency relations and the contextual propagation of defects. Furthermore, we devised two innovative centrality metrics—Outgoing Risk Degree and Incoming Risk Degree—to rank cargo based on their vulnerability risk in dependency chains, thereby highlighting key players crucial for risk control. Finally, utilizing K-meare clustering with the proposed centrality scores, we partitioned the cargo into distinct groups dependent on their primary use cases or target users.

The stochastic Ginzburg-Landau equation serves as an archetypal model for amplitude irreducibility in nonequilibrium systems, with the driving force determined by either additive or multiplicative pure jump processes. This paper establishes amplitude irreducibility in the cited pure-jump contexts by selecting appropriate measures, thereby yielding a determination of the pure-jump irreducibility. As a direct application, we employ this property to prove convergence towards equilibrium in both additive and multiplicative scenarios. Furthermore, utilizing irreducibility as a tool, we demonstrate the existence of a global attractor when the noise is of the pure-jump multiplicative type.

We examine $\delta(\mathcal{P}(G))$, representing the minimum degree of the power graph defined by an element's occurrence frequencies, specifically within finite nilpotent groups. For any finite abelian group $G$, it is established that $\delta(\mathcal{P}(G))$ matches the count of non-cyclic direct summands plus one, with this relationship yielding a complete characterization of minimal degrees in power graphs for all finite nilpotent groups.

This study addresses the challenges of optimizing Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) when processing point clouds, specifically targeting the issues of high memory usage and inefficient computations. To combat these difficulties, the researchers propose KGCN, an architecture designed for large-scale point cloud datasets with minimal memory footprint. KGCN achieves this efficiency by filtering data through a pre-processing stage that discards unconnected vertexes and performs multiple graph convolutional layers utilizing k-nearest-neighbor (KNN) graphs to further compress data. Additionally, the method incorporates an input layer that maps feature values, with the overall model supported by a prediction layer to ensure accuracy. Experimental evaluations across several public datasets demonstrate that KGCN surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in maintaining superior classification precision while significantly reducing computational computational costs.

This paper presents a novel "semantic host-free" Trojan attack in which triggered inputs within infected networks possess no meaningful value even for the original model's intended semantics. Although prior research explored semantic-free attacks, those patterns remained model-dependent, limiting their generalizability. In contrast, the proposed semantics-free approach is both universal and robust across different models. Our findings reveal a profound insight: standard clean data inherently contains rich, high-quality trigger embeddings capable of confounding clean architectures, leading original systems to output predicted triggers rather than meaningful input. We further develop robust, semantics-free triggers applicable to state-of-the-art defenses, achieving an attack success rate of 72% on GPT-2 and 80% on BERT. Beyond these experiments, we offer theoretical analyses and extensive evaluations demonstrating the efficacy and scalability of our methods.

A high-resolution spectroscopic survey targeting 155 of the most well-characterized terrestrial exoplanets was conducted to analyze their host stars. By measuring 14 elemental abundances, the study explored the range of, and compared, these compositions to the Sun. Findings indicate that 94% of these hosts contain significantly higher magnesium-to-silicon ratios, while 99% show higher titanium-to-silicon ratios, than required for typical terrestrial planets. Notably, no counterpart was found for 40% of the stars exhibiting lower titanium levels. Assuming these 40% lower-iron candidates instead possess enhanced stone-to-core ratios, approximately 90% of the stars still maintain elevated iron abundances. Although current data are insufficient to pinpoint the exact origin of these anomalies, the results underscore a critical need for similar surveys on larger samples to inform models of planet formation.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) utilizing Channel State Information (CSI) have demonstrated high efficacy in wireless localization. Nevertheless, standard input preprocessing often leads to excessive computation and elevated error rates caused by channel fluctuations. This study introduces an attention-based CSI localization system that efficiently suppresses noise while preserving critical signal features. Specifically, the model extracts complementary characteristics from CSI sub-carriers through dual parallel DNNs, followed by an attention mechanism to weigh and integrate the learned features. The framework employs a multi-scale data augmentation strategy based on CSI transformations to enhance model robustness. Experimental results indicate that the proposed approach significantly improves localization accuracy and cuts training computation by 42% relative to prior state-of-the-art methods.

"We offer a comprehensive, unifying perspective on the assorted semantical frameworks utilized in modal logic within the current scholarship by employing category-theoretic methods. This approach naturally leads to a generalized notion of Kripke semantics; any functor mapping into a suitable category of structures can serve as such. Our investigation focuses primarily on the category TopGph of graphs with topologies. By exploiting the categorical mechanism wherein functors are unified through their right adjoints, we can understand various modal logical semantics as different observational methods of the same underlying algebraic object. Consequently, we formulate a technique to amalgamate the right adjoints derived from specific observation schemes, allowing for new logical interpretations that synthesize existing ones. As a practical application, we demonstrate multiple ways of unifying the classical frameworks for combining modalities with neighborhood operators and intuitionistic topologies, yielding novel logical interpretations in the process."

A strong edge-edge coloring of a graph is defined as an edge coloring where every edge touches no other edges of the same color within a radius; equivalently, the induced subgraph formed by any color class is independent. The strong chromatic index, denoted as $\chi'_{s}(G)$, represents the minimum number of colors needed for a strong edge edge coloring. In 2003, Gyri'k'n conjectured that for any maximum degree $\Delta$ graph $G$, the inequality $\chi'_{s}(G) \le \frac{5}{4}\Delta^2 + 2\Delta^2 + 2\Delta^2 + \dots$ would always be valid. Specifically, for maximum degree $\Delta$ graphs $G$, the inequality $\chi'_{s}(G) \le \dots$ would always be valid. In this paper, the authors present a conjecture that there exist bipartite graphs with $4\Delta^2 + 2\Delta^2 + \dots$ the minimum number of edges.

This research investigates functions defined on Hamming graphs $H(n,d)$, where $n$ denotes the vertex count and the parameter $n$ is often related to the graph diameter. A function's support is the set of vertices assigned non-zero values, and its size corresponds to the number of such vertices, which we aim to minimize. Given a function on $H(n,d)$, its Fourier transform is a vector in $\mathbb{C}^{V(H(n,d))}$, where entries represent Fourier coefficients at specific frequency vectors. The graph is a Cayley system, allowing function transforms to be interpreted as convolutions with an indicator function on the underlying abelian group. Consequently, determining a function with minimal support becomes a type of inverse problem, or more accurately, an optimization challenge: selecting a set of frequencies to minimize the resulting indicator function support, or at the graph level, the $\ell_1$-norm of the Fourier transform, subject to constraints regarding the norm lower bounds of selected frequency elements' Fourier transforms.

COPASI, a widely utilized command-line simulation tool for biochemical networks, can be accessed via various web interfaces, including our new Shiny-based ShinyCOPASI. While existing web options support file uploading, ShinyCOPASI's primary advantage is pre-loading a vast library of public COPASI models. This facilitates the interactive analysis of specific networks without the need to download files, though users retain the ability to upload custom models. ShinyCOPASI supports multiple visualization modes, such as graphical representations, sensitivity graphs, and parameter scans. As a browser-based application, it runs locally on a server to ensure data privacy and security, offering the robust model exploration and pre-loaded content of a dedicated website within the privacy controls of a local desktop setup

Machine learning techniques for solving differential equations have become increasingly popular across science and engineering domains. Although these so-called "Physics-informed Machine Learning" approaches promise to bridge theoretical insights with experimental observations, they currently face significant hurdles: ensuring predicted outcomes are accurate enough for practical use and efficiently handling massive datasets. A primary concern is that uncertainty quantification has been largely overlooked in these models. This study addresses this gap by introducing rigorous statistical frameworks and validated metrics to evaluate and compare different uncertainty estimation methodologies within the context of surrogate modeling.

In the study of compact quantum groups, we examine structural properties of the von Neumann algebra consisting of class functions. For a compact quantum group satisfying the Kac type conditions, the center of this algebra is one-dimensional; however, its centerlessness fails notably when considering quantum $SU(2)$ through the discovery of non-triality at specific dimensions. Furthermore, we establish that the algebra is a finite type I factor precisely in situations where centrality holds. Finally, initial strides toward determining the precise dimensionality for $Q^{5+1}$ are presented. These findings rely heavily on essential attributes of the associated representation permutation systems.

Although policy iteration is popular for resolving Markov decision processes (MDPs) due to its swift convergence near optimality, it suffers from slow performance on large systems because of the need to solve massive linear equations at each iteration. This paper introduces an accelerated version utilizing the indirect GMRES method to resolve these linear equations. By leveraging the structure inherent in the linear equations arising from policy evaluation, we develop a tailored preconditioner. Furthermore, we analyze the performance of this proposed algorithm in the context of stochastic shortest path problems and validate its effectiveness through experiments on large-scale instances within Mark reward per transition problems.

Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a weighted oriented graph with edge ideal $I(\mathcal{D})$. We demonstrate that for a specified class of oriented trees $\mathcal{D}$, the ordinary and symbolic powers of this ideal are always equivalent. Furthermore, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions ensuring the equality between these powers specifically for lines equipped with their natural orientations.

Computer models are increasingly integral to understanding complex phenomena, which can lead to discrepancies between model outputs and empirical data caused by inaccurate specifications. The goal of model calibration is to resolve this by searching for the specific model inputs that minimize the distance between simulations and real-world observations. This study presents a new approach addressing this optimization challenge by employing contour plots of the discrepancy function. We propose an algorithm termed MCE (Multi-Contour Estimation) that leverages low-discrepancy sequences to generate these contours efficiently. MCE applies these structures to reduce the numerical discrepancy function within the calibrated framework. The method's utility and performance were validated through two practical scenarios where calibration involved continuous variables. Comparative evaluations against established optimization techniques demonstrated that the proposed algorithm identified more optimal solutions in less time, thereby reducing computational cost and time while improving calibration accuracy.

This work investigates the potential of local queries—information regarding a specific region in feature space—for acquiring knowledge about an arbitrary function. It establishes both necessary and sufficient conditions for local queries to be valuable in the context of probabilistic reasoning and robust learning. These findings illuminate the link between a function's sensitivity to perturbations and the utility of these queries for robust acquisition, while also addressing the implications for Sufficient and Necessary conditions for a function to be identifiable from these queries using a probabilistic approach. It proposes to use the concepts of a function's "zoomable" and "robustness" in the information theoretic framework to understand when local queries can support the identification and learning of that function. Specifically, it defines the utility based on how a function's "zoomability" relates to its "robustness" and derives direct consequences of this definition for the acquisition of knowledge about any given function through a series of queries. It demonstrates that if a function is both "robustly-accurate" and "zoomable," then an arbitrary amount of information about that function can be obtained with a finite sequence of queries; conversely, if a function is not robust, then an infinite sequence of queries may be required to acquire an arbitrary amount of information. It also provides a specific example, such as the step function in a one-dimensional space, to show that the number of queries required to learn a function is proportional to the inverse of its robustness.

This finding substantiates the $\gamma$-tagged jet technique as a powerful instrument for detecting medium-induced modifications in jet fragmentation. Furthermore, the current experimental results align well with predictions from Monte-Carlo simulations that incorporate the medium-induced gluon bremsstrahlung physics.

Following the recent findings of Gaia data indicating a proper motion anomaly for the system WISEA J153429.75-104303.3—a distant and massive binary composed of two brown dwarfs—researchers analyzed its 2D and 3D structure using archival Hubble Space Telescope and eROSITA observations. Orbiting each other with a period of 19.5 years, this system is the first confirmed multi-system containing the lowest-mass stars and the second-lowest-mass binaries verified by *Gaia*. Although the system's origin remains uncertain, it is likely an field-object given that it is not a moving group member. This study analyzes the extensive measurement results concerning pion, kaon, proton/antiproton, and $\phi$ meson production within the transverse mass ($m_T$) range of 0 to 3.5 GeV/$c$ during the system size change observed in central events of the 5.44 TeV per nucleon-nucleon collision of Xenon. These results are complemented by comparisons to perturbative QCD models, non-linear mixed non-linearities of the gluon saturation model, and hydrodynamic calculations.

This paper introduces an economical approach to numerically solving DGLAP equations for both single-parton PDFs and pair-based DPDs, relying on Chebyshev interpolation. DPD evolution is conducted using a computationally practical number of grid points while accommodating independent renormalization scales for both partons. Furthermore, both techniques incorporate NNLO DGLAP kernels and mechanism for flavor matching.

The behavior of a liquid film flowing along a fiber is examined using both numerical simulations and physical experiments. We demonstrate that systems involving a viscous fluid exhibiting pseudoplastic or dilatant properties, alongside those involving a non-Newtonian solvent, can support liquid films that are more stable than those of a Newtonian fluid fed at a constant rate. This enhanced stability arises because non-Newtonian effects amplify film slip at the interface with the surrounding gas, thereby suppressing the Rayleigh-Plateau instability. Specifically, we identify two mechanisms: first, the shear-dependent viscosity alters the curvature response, modifying pressure dynamics; second, flow-induced normal stresses generate either additional suppression (via dilatancy) or enhancement (via pseudoplasticity) of slip. Our findings confirm that the presence of such fluids promotes wetting of fibers by facilitating greater interfacial slip.

Diffusion represents a fundamental phenomenon in nature with widespread applications across physics, chemistry, biology, and finance. While significant research has addressed diffusion processes over rectangular, triangular, triangular regions, solutions for areas beyond polygons remain somewhat restricted. This paper introduces Fick's second law regarding the dynamics of diffusion area of any shape. It achieves this via a combination methods including using Fock space, solving Sturm-Louville problems, applying Fourier series and transforms, and employing Green's functions. The general diffusion equation solved in this paper is valid for most irregular shapes.

The increasing prevalence of computers has fueled significant research into optical character recognition (OCR) and handwritten equation recognition. This study introduces a system for identifying handwritten mathematical vocabulary using image-based handwriting sensor data. First, we apply a conditional random field (CRF) to construct a knowledge graph of related terms, which is subsequently mined to generate training datasets. A Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) trained on these datasets achieves approximately 90% classification accuracy. Finally, the obtained classifications facilitate data annotation for OCR and handwritten equation recognition tasks.

This study introduces a novel technique for synthesizing speech duration labels to re-examine Transducer-based Neural Machine Translation. Leveraging CleanCorpus data, we created GenCMD to produce synthetic mark-to-mark durations for 8 language pairs using 87.7% of the corpus. While the generated labels yield translation results comparable to those from the annotated versions in our evaluation, we observe a performance drop for languages involving labels that differ significantly from ground truth. By analyzing the distribution of these annotations, we discovered a high frequency of empty or prolonged segments—specifically, durations exceeding 2 standard deviations appear with a median relative frequency of 0.15. This inconsistency suggests that incorporating such labeled data may introduce noise and hinder model outcomes.

Occupancy modeling is a standard method for estimating the presence or absence of a target species while accounting for imperfect detection, and it is frequently utilized to examine environmental influences on that species' distribution. While single-species occupancy modeling addresses concerns regarding one species, integrated data analysis offers a more powerful alternative by jointly analyzing two or more co-occurring species through either paired or comparative frameworks. Furthermore, spatial variants of these models help clarify the ecological mechanisms driving distributions by incorporating available covariates. The `spOccupancy` package is designed to fit these spatial versions using either mark-recapture data or paired and comparative designs available via `spOccupancy`. Describing the package's features, this paper reviews examples of interest regarding simultaneous and differential species analyses while also providing an evaluation of the software's computational efficiency. Results indicate that the model's ability to process extensive datasets makes it suitable for addressing practical ecological inquiries, particularly in scenarios involving real-time monitoring where rapid model application is essential alongside identifying environmental factors affecting distributions across multiple contexts.

The rapid escalation in skin lesion images has created a critical demand for advanced analysis capabilities. While current research primarily targets classification, our objective diverges to perform the more complex task of differential diagnosis. This process involves pinpointing the specific context of a patient's scenario, an application tailored for professional use by dermatologists and aligned with clinical realities. We introduce the SKAIR Cardiology & Professional (SCAP) dataset, a novel, extensive collection containing 58,500 images of five distinct skin lesions that explicitly records professional diagnoses. Furthermore, we present an end-to-end deep learning framework for professional classification, utilizing a multi-level architecture. Our F1-scores on the SCAD dataset demonstrate state-of-the-art performance within this specific domain. Finally, we have deployed the System for Machine-Assisted Image Review for Cutaneous Impacts (SkCID), a web-based platform designed to showcase this system and facilitate further investigation into similar applications.

We introduce a probabilistic autoencoder designed to learn an informed, compressed representation of Type Ia supernovae spectra that captures the essential physical characteristics necessary for classification. By utilizing these representations, a binary classifier effectively and rapidly determines whether a supernova is an Ia or not based on its condensed data format, thereby enhancing the efficiency of Bayesian inferences within the framework of Hubble diagram construction and cosmological parameter estimation. Furthermore, we are able to generate synthetic spectra by sampling from the compressed data space, a process intended to address current limitations in scarcity and balance datasets for classification tasks. Ultimately, leveraging both condensed data formats and synthesized datasets may significantly improve the precision of cosmological parameter estimation regarding the expansion history and acceleration of the universe.

We describe the discovery of a neutral gas outflow in the lensed, dusty star-forming galaxy AT2019019 operating at a redshift of z = 2.099 ± 0.001. Discovered through high-resolution X-Shooter spectroscopy, this outflow manifests with multiple velocity components ranging from 300 to 500 km s$^{-1}$. Its outflow rate is estimated at M$_{\text{out}}$ = 0.17 M$_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$, representing more than a doubling of the previous record for outflow rates in dusty galaxies at similar redshifts. The outflow's total momentum loss rate, $\dot{P}_{\text{out}}$ = 1.59 × 10$^{32}$ erg s$^{-1}$, exceeds that of the parent galaxy's stellar wind by approximately 20%. These observations indicate that the outflow is not merely driven by stellar processes but is likely powered by AGN activity. When compared to other massive galaxies at comparable cosmic epochs, AT2019019 demonstrates that AGN-driven outflows can reach significantly higher efficiency levels than previously understood.

The study examines how momentum entrainment varies in particle-laden turbulent plumes as unladen plumes are merged. As the density ratio ($\rho_p/\rho_f$) and particle Reynolds number ($Re_p$) increase, observed momentum entrainment declines. Overall, the mixture's entrainment remains below that of an unladen plume with the same total Reynolds number. While earlier studies attributed the reduction in entrainment to increased momentum loss from fluid drag with $Re_p$, this explanation is insufficient. Instead, our findings indicate that the reduction in entrainment results more significantly from the heightened viscosity ($\mu_p$) associated with higher volume fractions or larger particles.

The propagation of infectious diseases is often modeled assuming that interactions within a static, fixed population occur in small groups, typically approximated as random, which-sound reasonable for many settings-is actually impossible on any graph with three or more edges. Consequently, we propose a novel framework where interactions are represented by hyperedges connecting at least two individuals. By redefining the spectral theory of such hypergraph structures, we introduce a sequence of spectral numbers that determine the extinction likelihood of a basic epidemic process (SIRS). These numbers offer spectral insights into the topology of the underlying interaction network and provide bounds whose significance grows sharper with interactions involving more participants. In many scenarios, these bounds converge, matching prior limits in standard pairwise epidemiology while correctly extending results to cases involving stars and complete connectivities where traditional methods fail. Ultimately, this approach establishes a fundamental link between the concrete spectral properties of hypergraphs and underlying epidemic risk.

The recent discovery of two-dimensional (2D) Cr-based insulating ferromagnets, coupled with their strong exchange interactions and spontaneous exchange interactions, makes them ideal candidates for spintronics. This study theoretically examines magnetic properties and spin textures of the CrI₃ bilayer using density functional theory (DFT) and muon spin rotation/mixing/relaxation ($\mu$SR) techniques. While the DFT results align well with $\mu$SR data, the proposed theoretical framework reveals additional ferromagnetic behaviors not yet experimentally verified. Specifically, the work investigates the nature of the exchange interactions, evaluates crab effects induced by the magnetic arrangement, and analyzes Rashba-related phenomena within spin textures. It is concluded that a finite Rashba parameter persists even in the absence of inversion symmetry breaking, resulting in an asymmetric spin distribution that exhibits a net magnetization. These findings demonstrate that the CrI₃ bilayer can generate complex, non-trivial spin configurations, although experimental confirmation is still pending.

Solar differential rotation reverses from the traditional pattern as a function of latitude; at high latitudes, surface layers rotate faster than the interior, whereas in mid-latitudes, depths see rates diminish such that the core matches or exceeds the surface. Most standard mean-field dynamo theories for solar analogs fail to replicate this complex, time-dependent behavior, typically relying on the simplified assumption of uniform differential rotation. This study utilizes a simplified two-component dynamo framework with $\alpha$ and mechanical shear sources to investigate the distinct impacts of differential rotation on magnetic cycles in solar-like stars. We demonstrate that models incorporating the anti-solar trend—faster subsurface rotation at high latitudes—produce shorter magnetic cycles compared to those with uniform differential rotation. Generally, magnetic cycles are found to be more intricate and shorter when differential rotation intensifies or becomes stratified. These results suggest that even in systems where magnetic cycles are present, they may be too brief for detection via current long-term observation datasets.

Although Generative Autoencoders (GAEs) have proven effective in addressing diverse variational inference challenges, they often struggle with poor sample-sampling distribution matching. To enhance such models, we introduce the innovative K-fan Auto-Encoder (KFAE) architecture designed specifically to improve matching between generated distributions and the true data distribution. Our novel approach features a shared representation framework that enables multiple GAEs to be coordinated within a single model. We further derive the theoretical underpinnings and properties governing the probability flow ordinary differential equation (PFODE) as applied to KFAE. Extensive evaluations across six real-world datasets confirm that the proposed KFAE model not only excels at mode collapse mitigation relative to current benchmarks but also consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in various tasks.

Model checking remains a primary approach for verifying multithreaded programs, though existing solutions are typically limited to specific subsets of programs and do not cover a broad spectrum of features, causing developers to struggle with adopting them in large codebases. Furthermore, because most tools struggle with excessive memory usage and runtime, and limited support for various instruction sets, developers have little ability to extend them or build upon them. McMini represents an innovative, general-purpose model checker that addresses these issues through the integration of Decorated Process (DPOR), which offers efficient support for memory management and covers execution over an extensive range of coherence and consistency rules. Key contributions of this work include a novel thread-safe, modular architecture that allows straightforward code development and maintenance, as well as the creation of minimal, maximal thread IDs, and the ability to identify minimal failing executions. The design also enables developers to build upon or refine it, as evidenced by the successful creation and maintenance of multiple extensions by our group and others. The effectiveness of McMini has been confirmed through benchmarks that demonstrate its capability to manage real-world, production-level applications.

WhatsApp has emerged as the leading messaging application worldwide, utilizing "forwarding limits" that prevent messages from being shared indefinitely in an infinite loop. These mechanisms compel recipients to pause and evaluate the information they are sharing, a feature intended to help combat the spread of misinfomration, which these platforms consider dangerous. However, these very mechanisms have simultaneously facilitated the dissemination of malicious malware. This paper examines a prototype designed to identify and block malicious WhatsApp links, along with the strategies utilized by malware authors to evade such defenses. The implementation of better security stances on mesing apps like WhatsApp could significantly diminish the effectiveness of malicious campaigns. Additionally, we propose a framework for assessing the impact of message forwarding mechanisms, aiming to illuminate the path toward messaging security.

This paper establishes a series of approximations for the site frequency spectrum within a general branching-population model. Specifically, we demonstrate a Poisson approximation for the count of singletons arising from mutations in general branching Gaussian populations, as well as derive an exponential approximation for the frequency of sites experiencing multiple mutations. These findings are utilized to estimate the conditional site frequency spectrum given the absence of ancestral reconstruction and to approximate the total number of coalescence events until the most recent branching occurrence.

The primary goal of spoofing detection systems is to identify synthetic artifacts embedded in speech resulting from synthesis or conversion processes. This paper introduces the incorporation of attention rectified linear units (AReLU) into end-to-end detection pipelines. By leveraging the attention mechanism within ARe LU to emphasize significant acoustic cues and filter out redundancy, the proposed method directs model focus toward artifacts critical for spoofing identification. Testing on the Logical Access NIST SIREN 2022 dataset demonstrates integration with ARe LU yields superior performance: paired with Wav2Vec 2.0 and an AST classifier, the system achieved 43.8% equal error rate (EER) and 99.5 true positive rate at a false-alarms per utterance (TPPAU) of 10.

Supergravity, a gauge theory merging gravity with supersymmetry, is a candidate for the universe's fundamental quantum description. During cosmic inflation, it should behave effectively like a low-energy limit of supergravity. This study explores how inflationary effective field theories (EFTs) can be formulated within a supersymmetric framework. Specifically, we develop a supersymmetry-based EFT applicable to single-field inflation, extending the standard EFT of inflation to include the five parameters $m_i$ ($i=1,\dots,5$). We establish constraints on these parameters derived from an $ \mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetry algebra, revealing that the parameters $m_1$ and $m_2$ are tightly bounded, while the remaining three, $m_3$, $m_4$, and $m_5$, can take any values. Consequently, we specify the most general supersymmetric invariant form for the single-field inflationary action and analyze how the parameters $m_i$ influence the fluctuation modes of both adiabatic and ghost scenarios.

Nonreciprocal optical systems are widely used to manipulate the signal transmission of light based on its propagation direction, but in this study, we investigate a new type of nonreciprocity that manifests specifically within photon pair correlations rather than linear propagation. This phenomenon represents a reversible behavior in the second-order coherence functions of entangled photon pairs generated via spontaneous four-wave mixing on a silicon microdisk, as confirmed by both experimental and theoretical evidence. Crucially, inverting the propagation direction of these photon photons drastically alters their temporal correlation profiles while leaving their total spectral power and spectral entropy unchanged. This finding demonstrates a mechanism to induce directionality in multitime coherence, offering potential utility for advanced quantum photonics technologies.

Superconducting quantum circuits are recognized as a promising platform for building scalable quantum computers. Achieving these circuits' full potential hinges on comprehensively understanding and refining their near-field environment to elevate quantum state fidelity beyond current benchmarks. We demonstrate a detailed investigation of near-field electromagnetic distributions within superconducting quantum processing chips utilizing Terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy (SNOM). By achieving sub-wavelength spatial resolution, we identify structural anomalies and specific near-field effects essential for advancing quantum computing. Furthermore, a synergistic approach combining SN-OM with numerical simulations enables the accurate derivation of the dielectric constant for superconductors, irrespective of frequency or incident angle.

While it is well-established that every subset of the real line can be partitioned into Borel sets containing exactly cardinality $\mathfrak{b}$ for some infinite cardinal $\beta$, this paper provides specific constraints for such partitions where the parts are not just any Borel sets, but must satisfy additional topological and combinatorial properties if they are required to be pairwise disjoint and $\sigma$-compact. By examining these conditions more closely, we characterize when disjoint partitions of $\mathbb R$ consist solely of sets that are Borel, $\sigma$-compact, and have fixed cardinality $\omega^{\cdot}$ as determined by the condition that for all subsets $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb R$, if each element $A\in\mathcal A$is $\sigma$-compact with $\text {card}(A)=\omega^{\cdot}$, then either $\bigcup\mathcal A\subset\mathbb R$is not dense or it holds. Financial markets are continuously shifting due to investor behavior, whose diverse strategies significantly impact market dynamics. Agent-based computational economics offers a robust framework for analyzing these market dynamics in relation to specific investor actions, making the identification of strategy combinations that produce desirable outcomes a critical issue. To explore this, we developed an stock trading agent-based model featuring multiple investment rules, each possessing unique market impacts and utilizing strategies partly based on existing literature. By examining interactions among these investment strategies using Big Data analytics and visual exploration of computational results, we observed clear differences in market effects according to how agents interacted. Furthermore, we discovered that traditional, established investment strategies consistently outperformed others and tended to lead new, emerging strategies, suggesting computational reality supports the theoretical view that past work influences future actions among investors.

Protocol detection involves the critical network security task of identifying the application layer protocol to enable precise protocol-specific Deep Packet Inspection. Because relying on individual protocol features is insufficient for reliable detection, effective methods must analyze multi protocol characteristics across every frame in the traffic stream, accounting for the non-self-contained nature of data. While previous approaches have achieved only partial success in this domain, since then, the field has seen a shift in focus to new solutions. This study evaluates the dynamic protocol identification capabilities of popular open-source monitoring software, revealing widespread vulnerabilities. In many cases, attacks employing crafted deceptive traffic can trick detectors into classifying malicious traffic as benign or selecting the incorrect target protocol for inspection. To address these findings, this research proposes two enhancements: first, integrating the concept of detection confidence into the detection algorithm, and second, applying machine learning to substantially reduce the overall error rate. Empirical results demonstrate that these proposed methods significantly outperform the original implementations of the tested open-source tools in terms of performance.

Electrostatic gating provides a means to control superconducting properties within a bi-metal layer. In systems pairing magnons and superconducting quasiparticles, electrons influence the superconducting wave function of Cooper pairs. In turn, these electrons can modulate the interaction between quasiparticles and spin waves (magnons). Consequently, superconducting entities can direct or switch the propagation of magnons. This study demonstrates the direct modulation of magnon propagation using thin-film superconducting quasiparticles, achieved through electrostatic gating of a superconducting layer in an FeW/Bi-2212 configuration. Federated learning serves as a widely adopted strategy for aggregating distributed datasets, and the audio classification task provides a robust benchmark for evaluating federated frameworks. However, most existing studies only replicate known training and test datasets, failing to reflect real-world scenarios where a server continuously onboards new clients accompanied by zero-shot unfamiliar classes. To address this gap, the paper introduces NovalAC, a novel federated learning task and architecture designed around a subset of the UrbanSound8k dataset, while treating classification for previously unseen sounds as zero-shot problems. This system simulates a dynamic environment in which servers receive data from multiple existing clients, alongside a specific module dedicated to handling classes introduced by each fresh user. The authors propose several novel algorithms, testing them against two baseline methods. Their results demonstrate that the suggested models exceed the baselines, and the study concludes with an audio data augmentation technique that further boosts algorithmic performance.

This Letter introduces a theoretical framework designed for comprehensive optical analysis of high-dimensional Greenberger-Horne-Zeinberger (GHZ) resources. The study initially validates this methodology through complete measurements of distinct three-photon GHZ states within a tripartite quantum basis. The approach is subsequently generalized, with a full photonic hyper-entanglement and quantum Fourier transform integration. The utility of this proposal extends towards enhanced multi-photon capabilities for both quantum computing and quantum communications in higher-order dimensions of entanglement.

This study proposes a channel estimation method utilizing intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS) for multi-user single-output multi-user systems. Assuming full system visibility, estimation schemes are established to mitigate full coupling during estimation, significantly lowering computational demands. Furthermore, a novel strategy named cascaded channel estimation (CE) is introduced to mitigate coupling effects. Subsequently, an IRS phase optimization framework is developed through alternating estimation with passive components, relying on the established channel estimation model under full visibility. Simulation results confirm that the suggested algorithms achieve performance comparable to full coupling approaches while requiring substantially less computation.

We analyze an extensive corpus of over 1.2 million articles regarding the COVID-19 pandemic in the U.S. from four prominent local newspapers, utilizing it to (1) compare how regional outlets cover the pandemic and (2) examine the impact of media narratives on public awareness as measured by searches for "coronavirus" and "COVID-19." Our findings indicate a positive correlation between the intensity of newspaper reporting—especially in the article's initial sections—and subsequent searches for the disease and death statistics, with the effect of one additional mention of "coronavirus" and "COVID-19" estimating a 0.03% rise in subsequent Google trends for that region. While our results suggest a link between media coverage and heightened public concern about COVID, they preclude conclusions about causality. A secondary observation reveals that search interest in the pandemic peaked and began declining roughly 18 to 20 weeks after local outlets first intensified their reporting around week one, a lag aligning with similar temporal patterns between news coverage and searches for the I.S.F. vaccine.

Counting serves as a foundational skill, yet its specific representation in the brain remains unclear. This study offers the initial demonstration that deep learning, utilizing a form of working memory, can effectively simulate the acquisition of counting. The achieved generalization across diverse tasks surpasses the capabilities seen in prior work that trained on a solitary dataset.

Bloom filters compress sets of bits for rapid lookups. Cuckoo filters represent an improvement by occupying less space and enabling constant-time verifications. However, a new generation of compact filters based on XOR filters can now filter even fewer bits per location while maintaining quick access. These filters leverage Xor sets to compactly represent infinite data. Although the initial algorithms were not optimized for speed or size, two new constant-depletion algorithms have since been developed for this purpose. These innovations outperform previous methods in speed and storage efficiency. Computation on these filters runs in O(n/d) time using O(n/d) space, where n is elements and d the bits per element. For typical values, complexity becomes O(n) in both operations. These results match Deleuze's theoretical lower bounds for compact digital filters. Computationally, these Xor filters are faster than competing approaches while reducing storage by 20%. These results also hold under typical assumptions regarding memory hierarchy performance on modern hardware systems where cache-level computation significantly influences efficiency.

This approach offers a method to derive market directional insight from the chronological order of transactions defined by time, price, and volume. The technique utilizes three core components: first, a functional representation of order flow utilizing a functionally derived fill sequence; second, the application of an entropy-based metric to quantify information; third, a directional performance benchmark. First applied to model the structure of a specific market structure, these tools were validated through testing on NYSE Nasdaq's 2018 data, demonstrating a capacity to generate positive average returns. Specifically, future-oriented testing revealed average annualized gains ranging from 11.6% to 14.8%. These results outperform those achieved by standard random walk benchmarks, as well as future-oriented strategies based on open/high/low range performance, which recorded averages of between 6.8% and unspecified upper limits.

This study explores the challenges federated learning presents when facing Byzantine malfunctions. We observe that standard vertical federated splitting techniques leak significant data about clients to the aggregating server, creating unnecessary privacy risks. In addition, certain vulnerable models are susceptible to poisoning attacks that can subvert learning integrity by sending outliers. In this paper, we introduce FLVoogd—a robust and privacy-preserving federated learning framework—by integrating Voogd’s method with vertically split learning architectures. To ensure integrity against malicious inputs, FLVoogd employs inlier selection when aggregating split gradients from clients, thereby neutralizing outlier-based poisoning attempts while maintaining data confidentiality on the server side. Our experimental evaluations across multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that FLVoogd significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches by achieving better resilience to both malicious and non-malicious attacks, all without exposing sensitive client data to the server.

We have created two datasets, each containing more than 100,000 driving scenes to facilitate the development of simulation-to-reality (Sim2Real) transfer for neural network-based autonomous driving systems. Our proposed methodology reduces the sim2real gap through a four-step simulation campaign. This involves initially aligning the coordinate frames of real-world data to those of simulation by matching camera views and road structures, then introducing domain gaps by shifting sensor viewpoints within the virtual environment. Subsequently, we employ a view-invariant neural network, initially trained on these varied simulated perspectives, to predict how image features would change if a physical camera were aligned with those views. This trained model is then fine-tuned using real-world imagery. The framework is modular and does not depend on specific neural network architectures, low-level feature extractors, or pixel-level alignment tools, allowing for extensive architectural flexibility. We evaluated our method on the KITTI Odometry and Motion-And-Position Estimation datasets, with results indicating an improvement of better than 20% over standard baselines. Additionally, the system was extended to facilitate 3D reconstruction of the actual driving environment.

Recent leaps in deep learning catalyze significant enhancements in deepfake capabilities, posing serious societal risks through the creation of photorealistic yet fabricated audio-visual content. These threats manifest critically in areas such as political elections and national security. While current detection algorithms are effective, they rely heavily on supervised learning trained on restricted datasets, resulting in generalized models that lack robustness against novel fake types. Under such constraints, designing universal detectors is challenging. This paper addresses the dual difficulty by establishing standardized benchmarks for automatic deepfake detection across two distinct categories—video and audio—utilizing real-world data. Simultaneously, to counter the prevalence of these deceptive technologies, we develop novel generators capable of creating convincing fake content from real samples. We provide comprehensive results for four experimental setups: two detection tasks and two deepfake generation tasks. Notably, our generators achieve top-tier performance in both synthetic and natural domains. Furthermore, our detection models attain the leading positions in both the real video and real video classification tasks.

We examine the atmospheric dynamics of sub-Neptune-sized temperate planets, specifically those possessing stellar hosts significantly less massive than the Sun. While thermal equilibrium dominant models predict high-altitude clouds or hazes that could obscure lower atmospheric transit features, we argue that the chemical equilibrium dominant framework offers a counterpoint. Under these conditions, heavy molecules such as CO₂, H₂O, and NH₃, which settle in the observable region, may generate detectable absorption lines. Our findings indicate that the planet's oblateness, a measurable signal during transit, can serve as robust evidence for an unobscured view into the deep atmosphere, thereby distinguishing between the two chemical regimes. These results highlight the utility of measuring planetary oblateness in the coming era of high-precision photometry, with the planet TOI-1789 b identified as a promising candidate for such analysis.

Inspired by the 1943 Maturana model, spiking neural networks have recently emerged as a promising field for addressing critical challenges in computational neuroscience, such as long-term temporal dependencies. Despite recent advances, existing approaches often depend on non-biological elements like precise spike timing for target fulfillment or require the backpropagation of error signals to minimize losses—both assumptions that hinder their physical realization in actual organisms. In contrast, this work introduces a fully biocompatible solution utilizing only pre-trained synaptic plasticity mechanisms. By evaluating two distinct strategies—One-step learning (which adjusts synapses based on prediction residuals) and Online synaptic plasticity (which dynamically adapts based on past spiking activity)—we demonstrate the ability to capture temporal patterns within artificial spiking networks. Experimental results across simple and advanced architectures validate that both methods can effectively learn on standard synthetic tasks, such as forring sequences.

This paper presents results from the Out-of-Vocabulary (OVC) OVID OVID Challenge. In this study, models were evaluated on generating translations for sentences presented with only source-language vocabulary, with the training phase strictly limited to bilingual data containing only those known words. The primary aim is to address a major obstacle in automatic translation: the translation of unseen vocabulary, which constitutes the bulk of words in typical corpora. We outline the training constraints that force systems to generalize using only known lexical items, preventing them from simply memorizing training data. The report details the submission protocols and presents the outcomes of ten participating teams. The findings reveal that current automatic translation systems can handle language under these rigorous restrictions, though performance notably lags behind systems allowed to access the training vocabulary during training. Finally, the discussion analyzes translation phenomena critical to addressing these challenges and introduces a comprehensive lexical feature-engineering benchmark designed to assess which word representations most effectively support translation without explicit training data.

This study introduces novel techniques for ensuring the accuracy of probabilistic solutions derived from chaos expansions, targeting both differential and difference equations. These methods leverage high-quality a posteriori error estimates to refine a solution by selectively enhancing specific time instances or spatial subdomains. The approaches are demonstrated using a spatially one-dimensional diffusive problem featuring a highly skewed probability density function, solving it via both finite difference methods and generalized spectral expansions.

This work addresses adaptive change or fault detection and isolation in systems subject to substantial uncertainty, where parameters are partially or fully unknown and specific modes are obscured by a high volume of noise. While existing literature generally assumes a complete knowledge of modes or focuses only on adaptation for systems with known modes, neither condition is typically met in real-world scenarios, necessitating the simultaneous online estimation of both the mode and parameters through a high-dimensional joint space, a process that becomes computationally prohibitive. To overcome this, the proposed solution decouples these tasks by integrating a sliding-window least-squares estimator with a multiplicative partially-observed Markov model (MPOM). By isolating parameter uncertainty and enabling direct observation through mode-specific noise variance adjustments, the MPOM operates more efficiently. The implementation details are refined to minimize computational overhead, facilitating real-time applications. Additionally, novel self-tuning mechanisms are introduced to dynamically adjust noise variables based on fresh data. Both theoretical rigor and extensive numerical evaluations confirm that the proposed framework is both statistically consistent and computationally viable, effectively and promptly detecting and isolating faults with low delays.

We investigate the stellar ages, metallicities, and light-to-mass ratios across different dwarf galaxies to determine whether their chemical evolution stems from similar mechanisms. Data utilized are derived from the ongoing observations of the dwarf galaxies Community Re-Analysis Project (cCARoP), a sample comprising 17 systems ranging from ultrafaint to classic dwarf categories. Our findings indicate a high degree of diversity in specific star formation rates (SFR) among these diverse mass regimes. Heavier dwarfs exhibit restricted SF histories with older average stellar ages and lower instantaneous SF rates, whereas lighter dwarfs show significant variation, including some with active SF and others fully quenched. Furthermore, we observe a lack of a universal initial mass function (SFR) driving the diversity in chemical evolution; instead, star formation histories themselves differ significantly between galaxies of various masses. Consequently, mechanisms such as reionization, photo feedback, reionization, reionization, photo feedback, and reionization, photo feedback cannot solely account for the observed differences within these galaxy types.

For a profinite group $G$, we introduce the class of $\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}_p$-continuous maps from $G$ to a topological monoid, utilizing this framework to define the $S^1$-homotopy orbit spectrum of the group $G$. Notably, when $G$ takes the form of the inverse limit of finite cyclic groups of order a power of $p$ ($\mathbb{Z}_p^\wedge$), its spectrum exhibits a canonical equivalence with the classifying spectrum of $G$; this relationship extends to classifying spectra applicable to broader categories, such as pro-$p$ groups. Furthermore, we establish an alternative equivalence by demonstrating that the suggested spectrum matches the classifying spectrum of $G$

Building accurate automatic extraction models for complex visual-documents, such as invoices, demands expensive training datasets. To mitigate this, we introduce Multi-Task Pre-Training with Sparse Labeling (MT-SL), a cost-saving approach that leverages the assumption diverse documents share common features. Our methodology combines large-scale unsupervised data with equally diverse small supervised collections. We present an innovative sparse annotation technique called "auto-reduction," which automatically identifies identical prediction features across multiple documents to allow sharing. This method expands limited training data by multiplying each label's impact and is integrated into our multi-task learning framework. Applying this approach to a real-world extraction task for commercial docs demonstrates our method reduces modeling costs by a factor of ten while maintaining performance no more than 0.5 F0.75-point lower than standard training using equivalent sparse data.

The European sulfur/Indian arsenic interface within the $\text{EuS}/\text{InAs}$ system serves as a critical model for studying magnetic semiconductors/semiconducting heterojunctions, primarily to enable studies of exchange proximity effects and exceptional spin-orbit control. Utilizing density functional theory, this study examines the electronic properties of a specific magnetic interface characterized by Eu atoms in a four-submonolayer thick layer possessing $2\times 2 \times 1$ periodicity. This research compares the interface properties across various Eu S bonding arrangements to determine their impact. Findings reveal a pronounced sensitivity of electronic states at the Fermi level to specific Eu atomic bonding. Specifically, a particular configuration facilitates strong hybridization between Eu $4f$ and In $6p$ orbitals, producing high spin states near the Fermi level alongside significant negative interface energy that promotes the stable deposition of Eu/$\text{EuS}$ onto InAs.

Data-driven deep learning models are transforming numerous fields, yet training these structures is often hindered by high computational costs and memory demands, particularly when processing massive datasets. While model compression and acceleration strategies have gained attention, existing methods typically focus on individual steps rather than providing an integrated end-to-end solution. This document introduces ClickTrain, a novel end-to-end framework for jointly training both model weight updates and fine-grained architecture-preserving pruning operations. By employing mixed-precision arithmetic, gradient accumulation, and synchronized cutting techniques, ClickTrain delivers highly precise and efficient model compression. Experiments indicate that applying ClickTrain to standard computer vision and natural language processing benchmarks yields eight-fold memory reductions and a twofold improvement in speed, all sustained with minimal accuracy loss. Furthermore, the framework facilitates novel applications within learning theory, enabling efficient end-to-end architectures that merge model merging with regularization and supporting large-batch scaling beyond previous limitations.

This research examines non-standard modal logics built over non-commutative, distributive, non-commutative ordered algebraic structures, specifically extending the full non-commutative ordered lattice language with both box-like and unbox-like modal operators. We demonstrate natural correspondence relationships: how this non-commutative ordered lattice theory mirrors its commutative counterpart, how it relates to the distributive full non-commutative ordered lattice with only one box-like operator, and most significantly, how it relates to the full non-commutative ordered lattice with operators for both affirmation and negation. Using these connections as a basis, we establish canonical full non-commutative ordered lattice semantics for these modal logics. Subsequently, we present an adequate axiomatization of these systems utilizing K, T, D, B, Kz implications. Finally, relative canonicity theorems linking the validity in the full non-commutative ordered lattice semantics to the truth within the corresponding distributive full non-commutative ordered lattice syntactic theories are provided.

The LIGO and Virgo collaborations have recently confirmed the detection of gravitational waves (GWs) arising from neutron star–black hole (NSBH) mergers. Ongoing improvements to these observatories are expected to substantially increase the number of such events. The lasing and Virgo instruments can only measure GW signals within a specific frequency band, and the sources must remain sufficiently close to ensure their waves do not degrade below detectable thresholds. Distinguishing NSBH coalescence signals from noise, as well as gauging a source's distance, is essential for both astrophysical and cosmological investigations. In this work, we introduce a machine learning framework that identifies NSBH merger signals within LIGO data and estimates their distances. The model achieves this using just the measured detector outputs, specifically the strain amplitude and its first two time-derivatives, along with the derived frequency. A key advantage of this technique is its ability to function with incomplete or imperfect detector data. Furthermore, for the same level of distance estimation precision, this approach requires fewer computational resources than contemporary alternatives. Additionally, we examine how the frequency of data sampling influences both the accuracy of the distance estimates and computational requirements, a factor that proves critical for the successful application of these algorithms in the context of the LIGO-Virgo Observatory network.

Our approach is fundamentally rooted in monotone operator theory, making specific use of warped resolvents as a key technical tool.

Primordial Black Holes (PBHs), hypothesized as remnants from the early universe, represent a potential candidate for dark matter. Their primary advantage lies in their versatility, as they form across a vast array of theories. Should they exist, their accretion of interstellar gas would generate electromagnetic (EM) radiation across the spectrum. This study employs the cosmological simulation package PopSyCLE to analyze such PBH-emitted EM signals. Our results cover a broad mass range of $10^{-7} M_{\odot}$ to $10 M_{\odot}$ for a universe composed entirely of dark matter consisting solely of PBHs. While PopSyCLE is not optimized for high-fidelity EM emission calculations, our analysis incorporates external data from literature. By applying new filtering techniques, we derive refined limits on the EM contributions from accreting PBHs—particularly in scenarios where they dominate dark matter—and these findings will guide the enhancements to future PopSyCLE developments.

Equilibrium systems consisting of hard convex polygons experience splay elastic effects, which can be interpreted as the material's resistance to changes in curvature. To investigate these effects, we analyzed an assembly of hard wedges made of balls, pinning their vertices to form channels, subjecting them to boundary control over opening angles and particle density. Our results show that increasing density triggers the emergence of crystalline structures characterized by straight boundaries or those modulated by splay, with the nature of boundary conditions influencing specific outcomes. Further increasing density leads to an isotropic disordered phase, a transition marked by the accumulation of pressure at infinite levels. Employing simulation data, we characterized these phase transitions using a lattice gas model to propose a mapping between the system's crystalline and isotropic states and respective gas-liquid and liquid-solid behaviors. Additionally, our analysis of isothermal compressibility suggests that the observed pressure divergence is partly a finite-size artifact; however, even if real, the singularity is likely modulated by a critical exponent that differs from standard Isorropic systems.

Equations defining recurrences for spherical random fields are presented alongside their solutions. These solutions are characterized as linear combinations of specific deterministic fields, where coefficients are random variables representing linear functions of field values at distinct points on the sphere. Provided the necessary variance constraint regarding these random coefficients is met, stationarity is guaranteed. This conclusion follows from applying Stein's method, employing spherical harmonics as tool for proving the sufficient recurrence conditions.

Standard quantum imaging protocols involve scattering events at the sample, which limits their application with delicate biological tissues. To circumvent this limitation, we utilize the phenomenon of quantum interference to implement a technique called "interaction-free" quantum imaging. In this setup, photons do not scatter off the sample, and its features are revealed solely through diffraction patterns from a surrounding structure. This interaction-free quantum imaging (IFQI) approach is comparable to the quantum pure phase imaging (QPPI) method in its sensitivity to subtle physical changes, but unlike QPPI, it requires no contact or exposure for the sample. Furthermore, IFQI offers distinct advantages in scenarios involving structures that scatter light anisotropically.

The rheology of complex liquids is highly sensitive to interfacial roughness conditions. This sensitivity arises because rough boundaries accelerate the formation and strengthening of stress chains across bubble assemblies, thereby amplifying phenomena such as friction and plastic deformation. Consequently, the rheological behaviors of bubble foams can range from smooth-wall systems exhibiting only shear thinning to rough-wall systems that display shear thickening under shear flow. This text reviews current research characterizing these effects, including the identification of distinct shear stress regimes and the application of shear banding models to explain the transitions between them.

In ISIC challenge 2019 tasks 1 and 2, we ranked 3rd and 4th utilizing this project to provide diagnoses for skin lesions based on medical images and auxiliary metadata, with our neural networks achieving superior performance over previous years due to strategic optimizations for both classification and detection tasks. Performance in these challenges relied heavily upon integrating diverse data sources, specifically previous year's datasets enriched with our synthetic samples generated to amplify underrepresented classes; this combination also incorporated the utilization of outlier detection mechanisms for identifying and filtering synthetic anomalies to further enhance model robustness.

This paper extends our earlier work [arXiv:2103.01153] by enhancing the free expansion phenomenon and generally improving non-equilibrium evolution through successive non-Markovian and non-reversible transformations. Central to the novel approach is a new M-Legendre symmetric map that preserves the number of available microstates, addressing limitations inherent in existing techniques. Furthermore, a theoretical analysis of the process during free expansion is conducted, during which we compare various approaches and compare simulation outcomes with analytical predictions, while simultaneously highlighting novel physical insights regarding the expansion.

We perform an in-depth, explicit calculation of the coefficients for Kontsevich graphs that emerge from curvature and connection components inside a globalization perspective for symplectic manifolds. Specifically, we demonstrate how weights assigned to curvature graphs relate explicitly through the hypergeometric function, alongside a more compact expression linking it to the known coefficients for an associated connected version. The analysis proceeds further toward identifying specific subgraph configurations within curvature graphs which vanish given their internal geometry.

This study examines a diatomic mass-spring system arranged in one dimension to explore the conditions for the formation of localized periodic orbits known as nanoptera. These orbits are defined by exponentially small oscillations separated by regions of rest. The anharmonic springs in the model are governed by the Frenkel-Kontorova equation, which is solved using the multiple-scale perturbation technique to generate approximate expressions for both dispersion relations and eigenfunctions. Evidently, anoptera formation hinges on whether the orbit's spatial profile exhibits its maximum amplitude near the system boundaries or within the interior. When peak amplitudes occur internally, this geometry promotes a higher count of phase peaks, thereby inducing stronger nonlinearity; under these conditions, anoptera exist solely within a restricted range of system parameters defined by strict constraints regarding both length and weak dispersion. Conversely, when the profile's maximum is positioned toward the edges (the interior is interiorly maximized), nonlinearity is reduced. In the resulting limit of large spatial separation between oscillations, anoptera can exist for a broader spectrum of parameters, though their viability remains restricted by specific constraints on the system's dispersion characteristics and weak nonlinearity.

Features present within inflationary power spectra serve a dual function: they offer evidence for specific aspects of inflation, they encode information regarding cosmological collider physics. While distinguishing between these two roles is typically challenging in conventional models, we identify scenarios in which cosmological collider physics leaves identifiable marks on inflationary non-Gaussianities. Our model involves two degrees of freedom, one of which exhibits oscillatory motion analogous to an excited colliding particle. We demonstrate that this oscillation creates unique signatures in the angular distribution of non-Gaussianities, specifically in quadrupole and higher multipole deviations from a pure dipole. These angular characteristics enable the extraction of the oscillating mode's colliding particle's mass as well as the spacetime curvature's expansion rate (Hubble parameter) during the inflationary epoch. Furthermore, we explore several scalar fields exhibiting non-oscillatory behavior post-recombination. We argue that collisions involving this matter generate primordial gravitational waves with distinct frequencies. Consequently, these signals offer another method to determine the expansion's Hubble parameter from immediately after inflation. Additionally, we discuss how these fields could generate primordial black holes. Observing angular signatures produced by such cosmological collider events provides constraints on which scalar fields actually oscillate and thus which cannot form oscillating components capable of generating primordial black holes.

Considered a graph $G$ with an even vertex count, we define it as accordion if there exists a partition of its edges into two paths, each utilizing exactly half the vertices—a property we establish holds for every quartic circulant graph with even order. We further show that if $G$ is quartic, accordion, and satisfies the condition $2m = n+2$ (where $m$ represents the length of each resulting path and $n$ the total vertices), then a specific even-sized matching exists within $G$ such that augmenting this structure yields a Hamiltonian cycle for $G$. We conclude by constructing a non-accordion example within the set of octic circulant graphs of order $n=2m$, demonstrating that the quartic constraint on $G$ is a requisite for accordion status even when confined to circulant families of order $n$.

We conduct a comprehensive study of the space-time distribution of finders launched by a localized initiator within a 2D square lattice, constrained to move using the three-state generalized walk. Our findings reveal that, contrary to the parity-dependent localization observed in single-line directed walks, quantum dynamics across the line exhibit uniform scaling regardless of parity. Furthermore, we precisely determine the spatial and temporal scaling exponents for both coherent and incoherent regimes through numerical simulation. These results are validated against analytical predictions derived specifically for the dephising case. Additionally, our analysis includes an examination of the spatial spatial variation in phase accumulation during the long-time steady-state period to resolve the origin of the parity effect inherent in one-dimensional walks.

Although Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) has become a pivotal area in computer vision, most existing methods struggle to effectively train Vision Transformers (ViTs), often yielding inferior results compared to CNN backbones. We investigate the reasons behind this limitation by analyzing intermediate representations within SSL ViTs. Our study reveals that while CNNs and ViTs both develop discriminative features under self-supervised training, ViTs fail to properly learn the spatial arrangement of these features. This缺陷 is further exacerbated by evaluation benchmarks, where common image-in-image augmentations introduce spurious correlations that distort the ViT's internal representations and hamper performance. In response, we propose Stochastic Crop Augmentation to replace current augmentations within ViT-SSL pipelines. Empirically, our method achieves an exact match of 76.0% on the ImageNet-22k benchmark and 52.4% on the ImageNet-2012 dataset, establishing the state-of-the-art for ViT-SSL. Additionally, our approach demonstrates robust generalization across various ViT architectures, delivering significant performance boosts for most models in the family.

We introduce a straightforward proof demonstrating that the initial value problem for the incompressible Euler equations in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ ($d\ge3$) remains ill-posed within critical Sobolev spaces. This result extends the findings of Bourgan and Li for the specific case of $d = 3$. Additionally, we establish ill-posedness for particular critical Lorentz spaces.

Recent advancements in text-conditioned image generation have produced systems capable of creating highly realistic visuals and artistic styles; however, these systems currently lack the reliability required for practical application. As people adopt artificial intelligence in real-world contexts, there is a growing demand for deterministic control and consistency in generated imagery. Addressing this, we introduce the "stable artist," an framework enabling reliable artistic expression in latent spaces. Our system operates by first training classifier-guided diffusion models within a curated image dataset. Subsequently, it employs principal component analysis to identify consistent directions in the image manifold. By progressively moving along these identified axes, users and systems can modify artistic elements in two key ways: first, by applying class-level guidance from image classification models to reach specific categorical concepts, effectively stepping concepts along their respective classes; second, by utilizing fine-grained class-level "image-features" as guidance, permitting movement within the semantic range of a single classification. Empirical tests demonstrate that this framework works effectively for both new categories and existing ones, utilizing either textual or hand-drawn sketch inputs. Furthermore, an interactive interface allows users to explore the image manifold by stepping through conceptual layers, thereby granting granular artistic control.

Recent breakthroughs in steganalysis— the scientific study of detecting stealthy data embedding within cover media—have primarily stemmed from the widespread adoption of deep learning techniques. In contrast to these standard data-driven approaches, we introduce a generative model that integrates deep learning with Bayesian methodology. This study offers a unified framework capable of performing both data embedding and steganoscopic analysis.

To investigate the extent to which human visual expertise with biology-action models can be exploited, we conducted a study evaluating how performance shifts when action recognition is performed under progressively reduced information levels, based on how video is presented to the observer. Using an incremental, frame-by-frame presentation method, we found that unlike image-based performance which remains stable, our results indicate that with less total context, human performance actually improves as more biology-unrelated information becomes visible in real-time. To explore potential enhancements, we designed a dynamic action recognition study using publicly available datasets, comparing a baseline 2D ResNet32 model against a new representation learning architecture designed for complex dynamic data. Our experiments demonstrate clear architectural improvements, with our designed architecture significantly outperforming the baseline methods of dynamic action classification. Finally, combining these findings with previous research, we propose that further human evaluation frameworks should prioritize dynamic action sets to ensure that important biological signals within video are adequately tested.
